Calculate the point where the ellipse $\frac{(x+4)^{2}}{6}+\frac{(y-3)^{2}}{9}=1$ intercepts the $x$-axis.

The $x$-intercept is $($
{{field-1}}
,
{{field-2}}$).$
feedback.worked_solution:
To calculate the $x$-intercept, we need to substitute $y=0$ into the equation of the ellipse and solve the resulting equation for $x.$ Doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x+4)^{2}}{6}+\frac{(y-3)^{2}}{9} & =1 \\ \frac{(x+4)^{2}}{6}+\frac{(0-3)^{2}}{9} & =1 \\ \frac{(x+4)^{2}}{6}+\frac{9}{9} & =1 \\ \frac{(x+4)^{2}}{6}+1 & =1 \\ \frac{(x+4)^{2}}{6} & =0 \\ (x+4)^{2} & =0 \\ x+4 & =0 \\ x & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the ellipse intercepts the $x$-axis at the point $(-4,0).$
